title: One input: does budget tightening predict productivity growth?
plain: Drew the best straight line from the size of a budget tightening (ΔCAPB) to TFP growth over the following two years, then tested it on countries the model had never seen.
lesson: The effect is real (negative and statistically significant), but as a predictor it is barely better than guessing the average. Significant is not the same as predictive.

title: Several inputs at once
plain: Added the four thesis controls and a yes/no consolidation flag, scaled the inputs using the training countries only, and trained with vectorized gradient descent. Repeated the unseen-country test and tried adding ΔCAPB².
lesson: The effect estimate moved close to the thesis, but prediction did not improve: a gain of about 9 % on one set of hidden countries turns into a loss when every country takes a turn. One test can flatter a model. Looking closely at the inputs also exposed and fixed a real error in two thesis controls.

title: A yes/no question: which consolidations are followed by weak growth?
plain: Switched from predicting a number to a yes/no answer: is a consolidation followed by below-median TFP growth? Used logistic regression with my own gradient descent, tried several regularization strengths (λ), and repeated the unseen-country tests. Then repeated everything with each episode compared with other countries in the same year. Finally added TFP growth before the episode (the pre-trend) as an input. Then fixed a leak in how λ was chosen, and ran a placebo test with the consolidation years shuffled.
lesson: Once a leak in how λ was chosen is fixed, the yes/no model does not beat the simple guess when every country takes a turn, with or without timing and pre-trend checks. A placebo test finds a faint pattern in the real consolidation years (only 2–3 % of shuffled versions get as many yes/no calls right), but it is far too weak to predict with and says nothing about cause. Leakage can hide in the tuning step.

title: A small neural network on the yes/no question
plain: Trained a tiny TensorFlow network (one ReLU hidden layer, linear output with from_logits, Adam, L2) on the same yes/no targets as Session 3, chose its size and λ on the training countries only, and compared it side by side with logistic regression in the same three unseen-country tests. Also checked how much the random seed matters, and tried three classes with softmax.
lesson: No gain. With every country hidden in turn the network is worse than the simple guess on both targets (−10.0 % and −1.9 %), and no better than logistic regression. One seed on one split looked good (72 % accuracy), but other seeds and the fairer tests do not back it up. With about 70 training rows even a tiny network has nearly one parameter per row: more flexibility adds parameters, not information.

title: Evaluating models and decision trees: is there a large-consolidation threshold?
plain: Part A (Week 3): training / cross-validation / test sets, bias and variance, learning curves, placebo tests, the log of trade openness as a rule for every country, and error analysis with precision and recall. Part B (Week 4): a single decision tree, a random forest and XGBoost on the yes/no question, a regression tree and a one-split ΔCAPB 'stump' on all country-years to look for a threshold, all with the same tests and a clean placebo.
lesson: On all country-years, growth afterwards falls clearly only above about 3.5 pp of tightening (a cut-off that barely moves when any country is left out), confirming Session 2's hint, but only 30 country-years lie above it, so it does not predict. Among consolidations, trees split on inflation, debt and trade openness, never on the size of the tightening. Random forests and XGBoost beat logistic regression on the original target, but a placebo shows the gain is not about the consolidations.

title: Natural groups and strange years: k-means and anomaly detection
plain: Grouped the 26 countries by their average trade openness, debt, inflation and growth with my own k-means (checked against scikit-learn), tested how stable the groups are, and compared growth after consolidations across groups. Then built an anomaly detector for country-years and tested it on the data quirks already known.
lesson: The clearest, most stable split is two groups: an older core (less open, more debt, slow growth) and catching-up or small open economies; finer groupings depend on the random start. The anomaly detector catches Bulgaria 1997 and Ireland 2010, 2011 and 2015, but misses Greece 2010, which is unusual only as a combination. It also points to new things to check, such as Ireland's TFP jumps in 2020–21. Both methods describe the data; neither says anything about cause.
